raw_response:
## Useful precedents for C26

The most direct precedents select compatible source before the compiler parses language-specific grammar. Compatibility helpers and source transformation offer complementary ways to reduce the number of maintained source trees. These are design-transfer candidates, not claims of a tested Swift implementation.

1. **C/C++ preprocessing with language-standard version macros** — https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-5.3.0/cpp/Standard-Predefined-Macros.html

   A numeric language-mode macro combined with preprocessing conditions lets one source file select the syntax appropriate to the compiler's selected dialect. The transferable distinction is between the language mode and the compiler's own release number. The GCC conditionals chapter also makes the parsing boundary explicit: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-3.0/cpp_4.html. Excluded text still needs valid tokenization, including terminated strings and comments. The version-pinned GCC 5.3 manual is supported by the official 2015-12-04 release date at https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-5/.

2. **GHC CPP compiler-version predicates** — https://downloads.haskell.org/ghc/7.10.2/docs/html/users_guide/options-phases.html

   GHC's version macros and minimum-version predicate provide a concrete model for selecting compatibility sections within a single package source file. Its documentation also shows guarding the predicate's existence for older compilers and describes preprocessing before the compiler proper. External preprocessing needs care around language-specific lexical rules. The opened manual is pinned to 7.10.2; an indexed excerpt of the official PDF states 2015-07-22, but I did not open that dated PDF.

3. **Clang feature and extension queries** — https://releases.llvm.org/3.7.0/tools/clang/docs/LanguageExtensions.html

   Feature-query conditions let package authors select syntax by actual language capability instead of maintaining a table of compiler version thresholds. Clang distinguishes standardized features enabled in the current mode from extensions. Transferring this mechanism requires stable feature identifiers and defined behavior on older compilers. Its archived 3.7 documentation is tied to the 2015-09-01 release announcement: https://lists.llvm.org/pipermail/llvm-announce/2015-September/000065.html.

4. **Boost.Config compatibility macros** — https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_60_0/libs/config/doc/html/boost_config/boost_macro_reference.html

   A shared compatibility vocabulary can centralize small syntax substitutions so library authors avoid repeating version checks throughout their source. The reference illustrates keywords and declarations that expand differently depending on support. This fits differences with usable older-language equivalents, but requires macro-like substitution and does not solve arbitrary grammar or semantic changes. The 1.60.0 release notes establish 2015-12-17 availability: https://www.boost.org/releases/1.60.0/.

5. **Six compatibility-library pattern** — https://pypi.org/project/six/1.10.0/

   A small compatibility library can concentrate version differences behind stable helpers while package authors keep most source within a shared syntax subset. The historical project page dates version 1.10.0 to 2015-10-07 and describes a single-file Python 2/3 compatibility library. Such helpers cannot make arbitrary new grammar parse on an old compiler. Detailed syntax-helper examples were read in the later 1.15.0 documentation at https://six.readthedocs.io/; those details are later evidence, and attempted 1.10.0 source opens were blocked.

6. **Babel 6 configurable source transformation** — https://babeljs.io/blog/2015/10/29/6.0.0

   A build-time transformation pipeline can derive compiler-compatible source from one maintained authoring form without maintaining separate release source trees. The dated 2015-10-29 announcement describes opt-in transforms and an ES2015 preset. This is an alternative when in-language guards cannot bridge grammar changes. Babel is a JavaScript tool, so transfer to Swift would require a separate parser/transform implementation, semantic checks, and usable diagnostics.

**Design implication, inferred from these precedents:** source-version compatibility needs an explicit decision about when inactive text stops being interpreted. A run-time condition is insufficient when an older parser rejects the syntax. A compiler-recognized guard, a prior preprocessing step, a common syntax subset with helpers, or a source transformation stage can address different parts of that problem. Any chosen approach should specify unknown-version or unknown-feature behavior and preserve useful source locations.
